titre: Tocqueville (1835): The “Tyranny of the Majority” Also Reaches Thought
accroche: For Tocqueville, the tyranny of the majority is not a rejection of voting: it also bears on the freedom to discuss.
contenu_vulgarise:
The expression “tyranny of the majority” is cited as a criticism of democracy by Alexis de Tocqueville. Chapter VII of *De la démocratie en Amérique* (*Democracy in America*, 1835), devoted to the omnipotence of the majority in the United States, says something else, and on a different ground from the one we imagine.

## A Principle, Not a Rejection

Tocqueville begins with a precaution: “I regard as impious and detestable the maxim that, in matters of government, the majority of a people has the right to do everything, and yet I place in the wills of the majority the origin of all powers.” The sovereignty of the people is not in question. What he refuses is that it should have no limit. The boundary he sets is “justice,” a law adopted “by the majority of all mankind.”

## Where Power Is Felt

The diagnosis is not limited to laws, which the majority makes and executes: it also bears, and strikingly so, on thought. “I know of no country where there reigns, in general, less independence of mind and true freedom of discussion than in America.” A king, he says, has only a material power that acts on actions. The majority has a force “at once material and moral,” which acts on the will as much as on deeds: as long as it is in doubt, people speak; as soon as it has pronounced, “everyone is silent.” He draws a consequence for literature: in his eyes, there is no literary genius without freedom of mind, and America did not yet have great writers.

## Guarantors Among the Founders

Tocqueville does not set himself up as a contradictor of the founding fathers: he cites Madison, in *The Federalist* No. 51, and Jefferson, whom he judges “the most powerful apostle that democracy has ever had,” according to whom “the tyranny of legislators” was, in 1789, the most formidable danger. The expression itself is not his: John Adams uses it in March 1788 to defend the separation of powers, and it is Tocqueville, then John Stuart Mill in *On Liberty* (1859), who made it known.

## The Shift

A note in the chapter specifies that Tocqueville is speaking here, as in all the rest, “not of the federal government, but of the particular governments of each state, which the majority directs despotically.” He is therefore not describing democracy in general, but a state of opinion in the American states of the 1830s. The remedies are the subject of the next chapter, on what tempers this tyranny.

It remains to be seen whether a majority that silences through opinion, and not only through law, still belongs to the vocabulary of tyranny.

carte.punch: Tocqueville does not fault voting for being unjust: he also describes the silence.
carte.idee: In Democracy in America (1835), Tocqueville places the origin of all powers in the majority, but refuses to let it have the right to do everything. He also describes how, once its decision is made, “everyone is silent.”

quiz.question: Besides laws, on what ground does Tocqueville describe the tyranny of the majority in this chapter?
choix: Freedom of thought and discussion, where the majority silences even before punishing
Elections, rigged in favor of the dominant party in each state
The right to vote, taken away by federal laws from religious minorities
The federal courts, which would always rule in the direction of the majority
quiz.explication: Tocqueville describes a moral force on thought: as long as the majority hesitates, people speak; afterward everyone is silent. He speaks of the particular states, not of the federal government, and does not blame electoral fraud.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What maxim does Tocqueville call “impious and detestable” at the start of the chapter?
choix: That the people should never vote on the laws they are called on to endure
That, in matters of government, the majority of a people has the right to do everything
That sovereignty can be expressed only through representatives, and not by the people
That justice must give way before the unanimous will of the voters
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Tocqueville refuses to let the majority have the right to do everything, while placing in its will the origin of all powers. The boundary he sets is justice.

quiz_supplementaire.question: According to the chapter's note, what is the real scope of Tocqueville's criticism?
choix: All the democracies of the world, regardless of political regime or era
The federal government alone, whose decisions are dictated by the national majority
The particular governments of each state, and not the federal government
Only the federal courts of the Union, which judge in the name of the majority
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The note specifies that Tocqueville is speaking of the particular governments of each state, which the majority directs despotically, and not of the federal government.
